I would rather have a single pole through out the entire surface. This may be what I am looking for to organize the strands, as they also are polar. If I can get a sheet of 2 poles per inch it would be simple to try and I will. This will also allow me to compare if diferent poles produce different result. I should only cover 2/3 of the plate such that 1/3 can act as a non magnetic base line.

This is an interesting idea, and I started doing a little research myself. I'm curious to see your results, but I'm not finding much that would suggest it would work. (But, hey, it doesn't hurt to try!)

I found this site, which is interesting:

[http://www.chem1.com/CQ/magscams.html](http://www.chem1.com/CQ/magscams.html)

There are a few nuggets of interest there, mostly to do with water. Scroll down to the light yellow table. There's a myth/answer there which goes like this:

myth:

"Water is a polar molecule, something like a little magnet"

answer:

"Water is indeed polar but this has nothing at all to do with magnetism. The polarity is due to the higher nuclear charge of oxygen, which displaces the shared bonding electrons towards the oxygen. This leaves the oxygen with a partial negative charge and the hydrogen with a partial positive charge. Water has no paramagnetic properties."

I imagine this answer might apply to gelatin, too.

-Phil

Well, I was thinking about MRI. I did a little more research and found this,

Diamagnetic Materials 

These materials are everything else ... plants, water, soil, wood, your skin ... all other substances. Diamagnetic substances show no visible reaction to the presence of a magnetic field, because the electrons in their atoms are spinning in equal numbers in opposite directions. These materials are magnetically neutral.

However, the molecules of these substances do have a very small polarity, because they are usually not symmetric; one end may have more electrons moving around it than another. When they are exposed to a strong magnetic field, they are repelled a tiny amount (rather than attracted). This has useful consequences. When human tissue, for example, is exposed to a strong magnetic field, some of the atoms move away; analysis of the movement is called magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, and is a useful diagnostic tool in medicine

[http://www.wcsscience.com/magnet/types/ofmagnetism.html](http://www.wcsscience.com/magnet/types/ofmagnetism.html)
